title: Knowledge check: URL Encoding and Path Normalization

questions.prompt: Which URL best expresses a resource-oriented interface for one order?
options: POST /v1/orders/{orderId}/delete is the default way to read an order.
GET /v1/orders/{orderId} identifies an individual order resource.
GET /v1/getOrderDetails?id={orderId} is always more resource-oriented because it uses a verb.
questions.answer_key: GET /v1/orders/{orderId} identifies an individual order resource.
questions.explanation: GET /v1/orders/{orderId} identifies an individual order resource. This is especially relevant to “URL Encoding and Path Normalization” because the API contract must remain explicit and reviewable.

questions.prompt: For the lesson “URL Encoding and Path Normalization”, which check provides the strongest practical evidence?
options: Test against production records so the exercise cannot be repeated safely.
Check that resource paths and relationships remain stable and do not expose implementation details.
Rely on a code review comment without running any representative check.
Run one happy-path call and skip invalid, denied, and failure scenarios.
questions.answer_key: Check that resource paths and relationships remain stable and do not expose implementation details.
questions.explanation: A useful check is repeatable, tied to an observable contract, and includes an important negative or boundary scenario.

questions.prompt: Which review warning is most relevant to “URL Encoding and Path Normalization”?
options: Paths mix resource identity with ad-hoc commands and inconsistent identifiers.
The expected behavior and relevant failure cases are documented.
A representative test can reproduce the result.
The API avoids exposing internal secrets and personal data.
questions.answer_key: Paths mix resource identity with ad-hoc commands and inconsistent identifiers.
questions.explanation: This finding weakens a core API guarantee and should be treated as a design or release issue, not only a style concern.
